notes.meaning: Boaz went straight to the town gate. In those days the gate was like the town's courthouse, where public business was settled. Just then the closer relative came by, and Boaz called him over. The writer calls him only "my friend," a phrase like "Mr. So-and-so." Some older writers think he is left unnamed because he refused to keep his dead relative's name alive.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read Ruth as a kind of fairy tale. In their view, "Mr. So-and-so" is a playful nonsense name, and Boaz beats him with clever words.

notes.meaning: Boaz asked ten town leaders, called elders, to sit with him. Two or three witnesses were usually enough. For big matters like marriage or passing on land, though, ten was the custom. Matthew Henry notes that Boaz did not settle his own case in private. He wanted it done openly and honestly.

Boaz explained that Naomi wanted to sell the field that had belonged to Elimelech. She was poor, and the family land needed to stay in the family. Boaz mentioned only Naomi at first. She was running the matter, and naming Ruth too soon would have hinted at the marriage duty before the first question was answered.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think Naomi was not selling the land itself. They think she was giving up her right to buy it back and use it, perhaps in return for support.

notes.meaning: Boaz gave the other man the first chance to buy back, or "redeem," the land, because he was the closer relative. Boaz could have quietly made the deal himself, but he played fair and did it in the open. Thinking it was only a land deal, the man quickly said yes.

Then Boaz added the catch. Whoever bought the land must also marry Ruth, Mahlon's widow. Their first son would carry on the dead man's name and inherit his land. That way Mahlon's family line would not be lost.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars debate whether this is really the brother-in-law marriage law of Deuteronomy 25, since Boaz was not Ruth's brother-in-law. Some suggest the deeper aim of that law was to protect widows.

notes.meaning: Now the man backed out. He said it would harm his own inheritance. He would pay for land that would go to Ruth's son, not to his own family. Or his estate might have to be split among more children. Matthew Henry compares him to people who speak well of faith but won't commit to it, for fear of what it might cost them in this world.

In those days a deal was sealed by taking off a sandal and handing it over. It was like saying, "The right to walk on this land as owner is now yours." The shaming part of the custom in Deuteronomy 25, where the widow spat in the man's face, was left out. This was a general custom, and the man had a reasonable excuse.

Boaz announced to everyone that he was buying all that had belonged to Elimelech and his two sons. Chilion's widow, Orpah, was not included, since she had stayed in Moab. Doing it so publicly protected the sale against any later cheating or doubts.

Boaz also declared that he was marrying Ruth so that Mahlon's name would not disappear from his town. By marrying her in public, he honoured Ruth and showed he was not ashamed of her. Matthew Henry sees in Boaz a picture of Jesus, our Redeemer. At great cost, Jesus bought back what we had lost and took outsiders like Ruth to be his own people.

The people gladly agreed to be witnesses and blessed the marriage. This was the usual wedding blessing. They prayed that Ruth would be like Rachel and Leah, whose children became the families of Israel. Ephrathah is another name for Bethlehem. They prayed that Boaz would do well and be honoured there.

They also prayed that Boaz's family would grow great like the family of Perez. Perez was the son of Judah and Tamar and the forefather of the people of Bethlehem. His family became one of the main clans of Judah, so the wish was for a family both honoured and large.

Boaz married Ruth, and the Lord gave her a son. Children are a gift from God. Boaz could marry a woman from Moab because Ruth had truly turned to Israel's God. Ruth had left everything to follow God, and she gained far more than she gave up.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the book was written partly to push back against the later ban on foreign wives in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah.

notes.meaning: The town women praised God for Naomi. The "kinsman-redeemer" here is the new baby, not Boaz. He would take away the shame of her empty home and care for her. Naomi had once called herself empty and bitter, but God had not left her alone after all.

The women said the child would bring joy back to Naomi's life and support her when she was old. They praised Ruth as "better than seven sons." Seven stood for a full, blessed family. God sometimes fills our losses through the people we expected least from, and love can prove stronger than family ties.
Naomi held the baby close and cared for him as her own. She was not his nursing mother. She was his loving caregiver. The woman who came home empty now had her arms full.

The neighbor women named the boy Obed, which means "servant" or "one who serves." It fit because he would care for his grandmother. Then comes the big surprise: Obed became the grandfather of King David. Much of the book was written to show this.

The book ends with a family list starting with Perez. He was the head of the branch of Judah that Elimelech and Boaz belonged to. The list proves that David came from the tribe of Judah. Ram is called Aram in Matthew's list of Jesus' ancestors.

The list runs from Nahshon, a leader of Judah in Moses' day, down through Salmon, Boaz and Obed to Jesse and David. Some generations are skipped, which was common in Bible family lists. These same names appear in Matthew's list of Jesus' ancestors. So Ruth, a foreigner, became part of the family line of the Savior.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars point out that Ruth is left out of this all-male list. They argue she is still the true hero of the book.
